sentenceSets.sentence: The minister arrogated to himself powers that properly belonged to the legislature.

answerChoices.reasoning: 'Usurp' means to seize power illegally; while both describe unjustified seizure, 'arrogate' emphasizes claiming without justification, while 'usurp' emphasizes illegal seizing.

'Appropriate' means to take for one's own use; while the minister appropriated powers, the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming, and 'appropriate' can mean simply taking without negative connotation.
'Assume' means to take on or begin; while the minister assumed powers, the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming, and 'assume' doesn't necessarily imply wrongdoing.
'Commandeer' means to seize for military or emergency use; while the minister seized powers, the sentence shows deliberate unjustified claiming, not emergency appropriation.
'Seize' means to take suddenly; while the minister seized powers, the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming—the reason this was wrong.
'Confiscate' means to take possession officially; while related, it typically implies official/legal taking, whereas 'arrogate' emphasizes unjustified claiming.
'Monopolize' means to have exclusive control; while the minister monopolized powers, the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming, not just exclusive holding.
'Exert' means to apply or bring to bear; the minister exerted powers, but the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming of them.
Relinquish means to give up or surrender; it is the opposite of the unjustified claiming the sentence describes.
Delegate means to authorize someone else to act; the sentence shows the minister taking powers, not delegating them.
Abdicate means to renounce or abandon; it is the opposite of the claiming behavior described in the sentence.

sentenceSets.sentence: Critics argued that the theorist had arrogated the work of earlier researchers, building his entire framework on their unacknowledged foundations.

answerChoices.reasoning: While 'plagiarized' means to present another's work as one's own, the sentence shows foundation-building (acknowledged or not), not direct copying; arrogation suggests claiming intellectual territory.
'Appropriated' means to take for one's own use; while he appropriated ideas, the sentence emphasizes unjustified claiming without acknowledgment.
'Usurped' means to seize power illegally; while he seized intellectual authority, the sentence shows idea-appropriation more than power-seizure.
'Misattributed' means to assign credit wrongly; while the work is unacknowledged, the sentence emphasizes arrogation (claiming without justification) rather than wrong attribution.
'Imitated' means to copy or mimic; while he copied ideas, the sentence emphasizes claiming them as his intellectual foundation.
'Absorbed' means to take in; while he absorbed earlier work, the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming without acknowledgment.
'Paraphrased' means to restate in one's own words; while he may have paraphrased, the sentence emphasizes unjustified claiming.
'Borrowed' can mean to take temporarily; while he borrowed ideas, the sentence emphasizes claiming them without justification.
Acknowledged means to recognize or admit; the sentence emphasizes the work was unacknowledged—the opposite of this distractor.
Cited means to quote or reference as evidence; the sentence emphasizes the work was unacknowledged, the opposite of citation.
Credited means to give recognition; the sentence emphasizes the work was unacknowledged, the opposite of crediting.

sentenceSets.sentence: The director arrogated the screenplay to herself despite the original writer's principal role, crediting herself as author when the industry awards rolled around.

answerChoices.reasoning: 'Assumed' means to take on; while she assumed authorship, the sentence emphasizes unjustified claiming—taking credit despite another's principal role.
'Usurped' means to seize power illegally; while she seized authorship, the sentence emphasizes claiming without justification in a professional/ethical context.
'Monopolized' means to have exclusive control; while she monopolized credit, the sentence emphasizes unjustified claiming of authorship.
'Proclaimed' means to announce or declare; while she proclaimed herself author, the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming, not just the announcement.
'Claimed' means to assert as true; while she claimed authorship, 'arrogated' emphasizes the unjustified nature and the spite toward the original writer.
'Declared' means to announce formally; while she declared herself author, the sentence emphasizes unjustified taking of credit.
To take credit means to accept recognition; while she took credit, 'arrogated' emphasizes the unjustified nature—taking what wasn't rightfully hers.
'Presented' means to introduce or offer; while she presented herself as author, the sentence emphasizes the unjustified claiming.
Acknowledged means to recognize or admit; the sentence shows she claimed sole authorship despite the original writer's role—the opposite of acknowledgment.
Attributed means to credit or assign to; she credited herself, not the original writer—the opposite of proper attribution.
Deferred means to yield to another's judgment; the sentence shows she took credit herself, the opposite of deferring to the original writer.
